question: What does this six-lecture synthesis actually establish about statistical learning, stability, mirror descent, benign overfitting, and implicit bias; which claims are faithful tutorials versus malformed transcriptions or overgeneralizations; can its figures and numerical illustrations be reproduced; and how current and distinctive is it relative to primary theory through 2026?

key_findings.claim: The work is a pedagogical synthesis of Nathan Srebro's July 2022 Les Houches lectures, not a paper introducing a new theorem, algorithm, dataset, or benchmark.
key_findings.evidence: The abstract promises an overview, the six lectures move from classical learning theory through benign overfitting and mirror descent to diagonal linear networks, and the acknowledgements identify the 2022 summer-school lectures and recordings. The central formal results are attributed reproductions of earlier papers rather than original results.

key_findings.claim: Its strongest contribution is a coherent teaching arc connecting hypothesis-class complexity, optimization geometry, mirror descent, function-space metrics, and kernel-to-rich implicit bias.
key_findings.evidence: Lectures 1-3 introduce inductive bias, benign overfitting, stochastic optimization, stability, and mirror descent; Lectures 4-6 then use Bregman geometry and KKT matching to discuss square- and logistic-loss dynamics. This organization is useful as a conceptual map even though many equations are not safe to reuse literally.

key_findings.claim: The introductory learning-rule and uniform-generalization displays suppress essential domains and assumptions.
key_findings.evidence: The learning rule is typed as acting on one example rather than a size-m sample. The ERM inequality is presented without loss boundedness or Lipschitzness, confidence dependence, approximation terms, or the usual two-sided uniform-deviation constants, and later language treats norm and complexity as almost interchangeable despite noting they need not be norms.

key_findings.claim: The no-free-lunch and regularization-frontier pictures omit conditions that change their literal meaning.
key_findings.evidence: The displayed no-free-lunch lower bound uses m divided by 2 times the cardinality of X but then says X may be infinite, where that expression is not a defined real-valued finite-domain bound. The regularization discussion says varying lambda reaches the entire loss-complexity Pareto frontier; a weighted sum reaches only supported Pareto points unless appropriate convexity assumptions hold.

key_findings.claim: Lecture 1 conflates ReLU, threshold networks, sigmoid conventions, VC dimension, and margin-style capacity.
key_findings.evidence: The text calls a threshold activation ReLU while writing a sign-network VC expression, defines sigmoid as one over one plus exp(z), which is the decreasing-sign convention, and says a bounded-norm normalized linear class has capacity B squared without specifying margin, fat-shattering, loss, or sample assumptions. The quoted network-capacity formulas likewise require activation, weight, depth, and computation-model conditions not stated in the display.

anchors.section: 1.3 Inductive bias in deep learning and activation examples

key_findings.claim: The computational-learning discussion incorrectly equates P not equal to NP with the existence of one-way functions.
key_findings.evidence: The notes write P not equal to NP, 'i.e.' one-way functions exist. One-way functions imply P not equal to NP, but the converse is not known. Nearby claims about no free lunch, efficient ERM, and TIME_T capacity also need explicit encodings, program-length bounds, and computational problems rather than the informal equivalences shown.

anchors.section: Computationally efficient learning and cryptographic hardness

key_findings.claim: The optimizer examples overstate minimum-norm selection beyond the assumptions of the cited results.
key_findings.evidence: Minimum Euclidean norm from zero initialization is standard for linear least-squares gradient methods, but the notes extend it without qualification to SGD, conjugate gradient, BFGS, and generic coordinate descent approximately minimizing l1. These conclusions depend on initialization, update selection, metric, step schedule, noise, and convergence; coordinate descent in particular does not generically select the minimum-l1 interpolator.

key_findings.claim: The matrix-completion and infinite-width ReLU summaries repeatedly turn conditional results into broad identities.
key_findings.evidence: The matrix-completion section correctly mentions counterexamples to universal nuclear-norm bias, yet a later rank-width story says the algorithm returns a nuclear-norm minimizer solely according to whether d is above k. The ReLU section says a wide shallow network approximates all functions and assigns a unique functional penalty without compact-domain, function-class, initialization, signed-measure, or loss qualifications.

key_findings.claim: The proposed hierarchy that architecture dominates optimization geometry while initialization, batch size, and step size are least significant is not established.
key_findings.evidence: The ranking is asserted after a set of heterogeneous examples rather than derived or evaluated. Direct work on initialization shape, stochastic diagonal bias, momentum, edge-of-stability steps, and parameterization-dependent infinite-width limits shows that these controls can change the selected predictor and learning regime qualitatively. Likewise, there is no single canonical infinite-size neural network: NTK, mean-field, and feature-learning limits depend on scaling and parameterization.

key_findings.claim: The Gaussian random-feature example is misnormalized and conflates finite coefficients with an RKHS element.
key_findings.evidence: With a uniformly random phase, cos(omega dot x plus theta) needs a square-root-of-two over square-root-d factor for the usual unbiased real random Fourier approximation; the displayed one over square-root-d mapping gives half the kernel. The optimizer then minimizes a finite vector w using RKHS-norm notation, blurring the Euclidean feature model and its limiting RKHS.

anchors.section: Gaussian kernel and random Fourier features

key_findings.claim: The double-descent section is an opinionated 2022 snapshot rather than a defensible current survey.
key_findings.evidence: It calls the 2019 Belkin paper arguably the first double-descent paper and says the phenomenon is 95 percent understood, overlooking older peaking literature and making an untestable percentage claim. The practical conclusion that one need not worry much about lambda is highly distribution-, spectrum-, noise-, and model-dependent.

anchors.section: Double descent and ridgeless least squares

key_findings.claim: Lecture 3's ERM and Rademacher displays contain type and probability errors.
key_findings.evidence: The regularized ERM minimizes over h while its objective is written in w and is subsequently called ERM rather than RERM. Uniform convergence constrains the norm of a scalar potential, and the high-probability Rademacher term uses square-root of 2 divided by delta rather than the standard logarithmic confidence dependence. These can be repaired, but not read as a precise theorem.

key_findings.claim: The finite-dataset SGD gradient is incorrectly identified with the population gradient.
key_findings.evidence: When an index is sampled uniformly from a fixed training set, the conditional expected stochastic gradient equals the empirical gradient, not the population gradient. The notes write the latter, then combine an empirical optimization bound with a population bound while leaving an empirical infimum on the right-hand side.

key_findings.claim: The direct stochastic-approximation step schedule grows as B times square-root t and cannot support the stated nonsmooth SGD rate.
key_findings.evidence: The notes prescribe eta_t equal to square-root of B squared times t, so the step grows without bound. Standard bounded-gradient convex SGD uses a decreasing schedule or a horizon-dependent constant of order B over G square-root T. The claimed hidden regularization and one-pass guarantee therefore do not follow from the displayed algorithm.

anchors.section: 3.2 Direct SA versus SGD on ERM

key_findings.claim: The projected-SGD presentation cannot make the projection optional under its own constrained guarantee.
key_findings.evidence: The algorithm compares against an l2 ball but says projection may be skipped because iterates implicitly converge to the set. Without assumptions on losses, gradients, steps, and dynamics, unprojected iterates need not remain in or converge to that ball, so the displayed rate lacks the bounded-iterate premise used to derive it.

anchors.section: Comparison of the two stochastic schemes

key_findings.claim: The stability theorem is ill-typed even though its intended leave-one-out argument is standard.
key_findings.evidence: The theorem evaluates the empirical objective with both a parameter and z_m although the objective was defined as a function of w alone. Its proof later uses the correctly typed empirical mean. Thus the conceptual route from symmetric stability to expected generalization is useful, but the displayed theorem is not a valid statement as written.

key_findings.claim: The regularized-ERM stability proposition is false under its stated assumptions and its proof reverses the minimizer inequality.
key_findings.evidence: Strong convexity of lambda times Psi does not make the sum strongly convex when f is an arbitrary Lipschitz nonconvex loss; convexity of f is missing. Moreover, because the leave-one-out solution minimizes its objective, its objective difference relative to the full-sample solution is nonpositive, whereas the proof writes it nonnegative. The next display subtracts an identical loss term from itself, so the claimed coefficient is not established by the printed proof.

anchors.section: 3.4 Strong convexity and RERM stability proposition

key_findings.claim: The strong-convexity and feature-map generalization calculation loses constants, domains, and powers.
key_findings.evidence: The proof drops the one-half in the strong-convexity lower bound and mixes m and m-minus-one normalizations. It optimizes a bound using sup Psi, often infinite, then informally substitutes Psi(w star). In the feature example, G equals gR, so the final dependence should retain g squared and the squared feature radius under the root; the display omits g and one power of the feature norm.

key_findings.claim: The entropic sample-complexity example contains an undefined p and omits the simplex domain.
key_findings.evidence: The entropy potential is only finite and strongly convex in the intended geometry on a positive simplex-like domain, which is not stated. Its sample-complexity line retains a division by p minus one even though p belongs to the preceding lp example and is undefined for entropy; the characteristic dependence should instead involve logarithmic dimension through the potential range.

key_findings.claim: The first mirror-descent derivation has projection and inverse-map typing mistakes.
key_findings.evidence: The Bregman projection is first written as a minimum value rather than an argmin point. Differentiable strong convexity alone does not guarantee a globally onto gradient inverse with the needed domain; standard mirror maps need Legendre-type conditions and careful constraints. The figure caption calls the inverse of the gradient simply Psi inverse.

key_findings.claim: The claimed recovery of linearized FTRL adds a vector gradient to a scalar objective.
key_findings.evidence: The final argmin includes the sum of scalar gradient inner products plus gradient Psi(w), a vector. It should include the scalar potential Psi(w), with step and regularization scaling consistent with the earlier FTRL definition. The printed equality is dimensionally invalid.

key_findings.claim: Lecture 4 reverses the sign in the Bregman divergence and therefore breaks the local natural-gradient derivation.
key_findings.evidence: Lecture 3 correctly defines D_Psi as Psi(w) minus Psi(w prime) minus the linear term. Lecture 4 changes that last sign to plus. Its Taylor expansion and metric interpretation then inherit wrong signs and omit the usual one-half factor, contradicting the previous lecture and destroying nonnegativity even for a quadratic potential away from a stationary base point.

key_findings.claim: The continuous-time mirror equations switch the descent sign and use inconsistent metric conventions.
key_findings.evidence: The discrete dual update has a negative gradient step, but the following differential display uses a positive gradient increment and an undefined Phi inverse. The notes alternately call the Hessian inverse and the Hessian itself rho and then write dynamics with rho inverse, so the same symbol does not consistently denote the local metric or its preconditioner.

anchors.section: Continuous-time mirror descent and metric tensor

key_findings.claim: The general steepest-descent examples do not follow from an unsquared l1 or l-infinity displacement penalty.
key_findings.evidence: Minimizing a linearized objective plus an unsquared norm penalty can yield the zero step or become unbounded depending on whether the dual gradient norm is below or above the penalty coefficient. It does not generically give coordinate descent or a fixed sign-gradient step without an explicit trust-region or squared/proximal construction.

key_findings.claim: The minimum-norm and mirror-manifold KKT derivations contain variable and dimension errors at their central conclusion.
key_findings.evidence: The Euclidean implicit-bias problem minimizes the norm of x rather than w. The mirror accumulated-gradient formula repeats the current gradient instead of summing past gradients, the Lagrangian uses undefined mu in y minus X mu, and stationarity subtracts scalar Psi(w0) from vector grad Psi(w) rather than subtracting grad Psi(w0). The statement that an m-dimensional trajectory manifold intersected with m constraints yields a unique solution also needs rank, transversality, and convexity assumptions.

anchors.section: Mirror KKT matching and general method

key_findings.claim: Lecture 5 begins with swapped population-loss arguments and a malformed homogeneity identity.
key_findings.evidence: The population loss applies f to w and y and passes x as the label, reversing the roles of input and target. Homogeneity is written F(cw)=c^D h_w instead of c^D F(w). The subsequent lazy-limit parameter-path statement cannot hold at t=0 as printed: w_alpha(0)=alpha w0 diverges from a fixed w_K(0) for nonzero w0. The primary result instead uses precise model/output scaling and centered paths or predictions under finite-time and regularity hypotheses.

key_findings.claim: After correction, the depth-two diagonal-network calculation does convey a valuable exact kernel-to-sparse implicit-bias example.
key_findings.evidence: For beta equal to w-plus squared minus w-minus squared under square-loss gradient flow and balanced initialization, the coordinate products are conserved. Integrating gives the hypentropy potential q(z)=2-sqrt(4+z squared)+z asinh(z/2); large initialization approaches l2 bias and vanishing initialization approaches l1 bias. This is a tutorial reproduction of Woodworth et al., not a new result.

key_findings.claim: The reproduced Woodworth Theorem 2 is materially mistranscribed.
key_findings.evidence: The small-alpha exponential condition multiplies by the l1 norm where the primary theorem divides by epsilon times that norm. The large-alpha conclusion compares against the l2 norm of the l1 minimizer, while the original compares against the minimum-l2 solution. The lecture then says alpha has to be exponentially small although the theorem gives sufficiency and the primary paper carefully separates a uniform necessity lemma.

anchors.section: Theorem 5.1, reproduced Theorem 2 from Woodworth et al.

key_findings.claim: The sparse-regression illustrations are not reproducible evidence and the statement that a kernel method cannot solve the task is too broad.
key_findings.evidence: The plots give a planted sparse linear problem and qualitative curves, but no code, data, exact sample draws, seeds, repetitions, intervals, optimizer tolerances, or numeric table. Their y-axis tick labels are absent. The shown minimum-l2 linear-kernel interpolator performs poorly in the chosen n much less than d regime; this does not prove that no kernel, tuned kernel, or regularized kernel method can exploit the structure.

key_findings.claim: The central function-space metric is inverted in the depth-two diagonal-network dynamics.
key_findings.evidence: For beta=w-plus squared minus w-minus squared, the pushforward preconditioner is proportional to w-plus squared plus w-minus squared, equal to sqrt(beta squared plus 4 alpha fourth). The Hessian metric is its reciprocal and the dynamics multiply the loss gradient by the square-root term. The notes instead declare rho inverse to be the reciprocal square root and then multiply by that reciprocal, while simultaneously interpreting large coefficients as moving faster and integrating the correct reciprocal Hessian. The preceding residual is also once written X transpose times beta minus y, and the quadratic for w-minus squared has both nonleading signs wrong even though its stated solution solves the corrected polynomial.

key_findings.claim: The explicit-regularizer polynomial does not have the claimed unique real root.
key_findings.evidence: At z=0 the printed quartic factors as u times (u minus 2) cubed, already giving distinct real roots 0 and 2. For positive z, direct root checks likewise produce two real branches. The relevant regularizer selects the minimum-distance branch, but neither the lecture nor the reproduced primary wording specifies that branch in the displayed definition.

key_findings.claim: The width-dependent matrix-factorization theorem is internally inconsistent in initialization scale, lifted shape, gradient sign, and regime classification.
key_findings.evidence: The lifted lower-left block repeats UV transpose rather than its transpose, so it is not symmetric. The symmetric gradient-flow display omits the descent minus sign. With entry variance alpha squared over square-root k, the variance of a diagonal UV product sum is alpha fourth, not alpha squared. The stated mu equality is dimensionally incompatible with that initialization. Most decisively, the first bullet says alpha little-o k to minus one-quarter is rich, while the third says the equivalent square-root k alpha squared tending to zero is kernel; the second uses big-O for kernel and overlaps the first. Woodworth's primary theorem instead places the transition in the lifted scale and calls the zero limit rich, finite nonzero limit intermediate, and divergent limit kernel.

anchors.section: Width theorem and three scaling bullets

key_findings.claim: The deep-diagonal derivation is unusable as printed because both branches are copied identically.
key_findings.evidence: The w-minus gradient incorrectly uses w-plus to power D minus one. Its integrated w-plus and w-minus expressions have the same inner sign, the beta formula subtracts identical terms, and h_D is defined as one identical term minus itself, so both beta and h_D are identically zero even though h_D is then called monotone and inverted. The primary Woodworth formula has opposite signs: h_D(z)=(1-z)^(-D/(D-2))-(1+z)^(-D/(D-2)).

anchors.section: 5.5 Deep diagonal gradient flow and integration

key_findings.claim: The deep result improperly includes D=2 and reverses the sparsity comparison of the l_{2/D} quasi-norm.
key_findings.evidence: The displayed formulas divide by D minus 2 and the primary theorem applies for D at least 3, yet the notes say all D at least 2. For D greater than 2, 2/D is below one and the corresponding quasi-norm is generally more, not less, sparsity promoting than l1. This explicit-bias statement is also distinct from the notes' corrected implicit l1 limit and should not be conflated with it.

anchors.section: Deep limit and explicit regularization comparison

key_findings.claim: The generic function-space Jacobian repeatedly has incompatible dimensions.
key_findings.evidence: F maps parameter dimension p to predictor dimension d, so a chosen Jacobian convention must yield a d by p map and a function-space pushforward J J transpose. The notes call it p by p in the linear section and write transpose-J times J while claiming a function-space operator. The later functional version inherits the same orientation ambiguity and calls a possibly singular tangent kernel a Riemannian metric without invertibility or a quotient/submanifold construction, making its metric formula unsafe without re-derivation.

key_findings.claim: Lecture 6 incorrectly says overparameterization d greater than n makes an arbitrary binary dataset separable.
key_findings.evidence: Oppositely labeled duplicate inputs are never linearly separable, and separability for d greater than n requires general-position or distributional assumptions. The max-margin directional convergence discussion also needs separability, appropriate loss tail, step size or flow conditions, and nondegenerate support vectors.

key_findings.claim: The logistic max-margin Lagrangian and gradient omit labels and use nonexistent indexed parameter vectors.
key_findings.evidence: Constraints involve y_i times the inner product of w and x_i, so stationarity gives w as a sum of nu_i y_i x_i. The notes instead write w_i inside constraints and omit y_i from the support-vector expansion. The exponential-tail gradient similarly omits both y_i factors and uses w_i instead of w.

key_findings.claim: The intuitive logistic-flow derivation reverses the exponential sign and contradicts its own support-vector conclusion.
key_findings.evidence: Substituting w_k approximately equal to g(k) w_infinity into exp of minus the margin should produce exp(-g(k) margin plus lower-order terms). The notes print a positive exponent, which makes larger margins grow faster, then claim those coefficients decrease faster. Margins and feasibility also drop y_i, and the remainder is asserted o(1) although standard asymptotics need more qualified bounded or slower residual terms.

key_findings.claim: The notes overstate homogeneous-network logistic bias as always reaching the global minimum-l2 solution.
key_findings.evidence: The reproduced theorem only says that under loss-to-zero, small-step, directional-convergence, homogeneity, and regularity assumptions, normalized limit points satisfy first-order/KKT conditions of a parameter-space margin problem. For nonconvex homogeneous networks KKT points need not be global minimizers, and initialization and optimization can affect which stationary point is reached. The prose immediately before the theorem says initialization does not matter at all and any homogeneous model always goes to the minimum l2 solution, which the theorem does not establish.

anchors.section: 6.3 Squared versus logistic loss and reproduced Theorem 6.1

key_findings.claim: The finite-accuracy logistic transition figure is explicitly conjectural and cannot support a quantitative scale claim.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 20 has no axes, dataset, sample count, optimizer, repetitions, uncertainty, or code. Its caption says the Q_alpha path is not proved and merely seems to hold empirically. The surrounding epsilon approximately exp(-alpha squared) and epsilon=10^-1700 language applies to a narrow diagonal classification construction, not logistic regression or deep networks generally.

key_findings.claim: The closing matrix-factorization section is a qualitative commutativity sketch, not a general implicit-bias theorem.
key_findings.evidence: The beta dynamics contain a typo using gradient of beta where gradient of the loss is required and inherit the earlier Jacobian orientation ambiguity. Replacing the factorization by an unrestricted positive-semidefinite lifted variable also omits the rank-at-most-k constraint unless width is large enough. A closed matrix-exponential or Hessian-manifold description requires commuting measurements and compatible residual gradients; the notes themselves concede that the noncommutative case can explore the full space and remains unsolved.

key_findings.claim: All 20 visuals render, but most are schematics and none constitutes a self-contained new empirical evaluation.
key_findings.evidence: The figures comprise architecture drawings, geometric cartoons, analytic function plots, borrowed or recreated matrix-completion and width curves, sparse-regression illustrations, and the conjectural logistic path. Several empirical-looking plots omit y tick values, protocols, citations in captions, uncertainty, or numeric tables. Inspecting every original PNG and every rendered PDF page found no corrupt visual, but also no evidence package from which any curve can be regenerated.

anchors.section: Figures 2-3 matrix completion and hidden units
Figures 18-19 deep diagonal network and depth effects

key_findings.claim: The exact current source is buildable but is not an executable research artifact.
key_findings.evidence: The source archive contains one main TeX file, bibliography and journal styles, auxiliary files, and 20 static PNGs. It has no code, notebook, environment, tests, raw data, seeds, or plot generators. The audited case-insensitive macOS build produces all 66 pages, but TeX requests uppercase Bregman.png while the tar stores lowercase bregman.png, so a clean case-sensitive Linux build is not portable without repair. Duplicate destination and layout warnings remain, and successful typesetting does not validate the malformed mathematics. Draft comments next to several derivations say the transcript is unclear, proofs or algebra should be copied from slides, or the authors do not yet understand what is being proved.

key_findings.claim: The current v2 revision is mainly an editorial expansion and did not correct the decisive mathematics; it introduced one additional Bregman sign error.
key_findings.evidence: A source-level v1-to-v2 comparison shows several hundred mostly formatting, prose, and citation edits and bibliography growth, while all 20 PNGs are byte-identical. The Woodworth threshold and comparator errors, width contradictions, h_D collapse, metric inversion, and logistic label/sign failures persist from v1. The repeated Bregman definition was correct in v1 but changed to the wrong plus sign in v2, so current-version status is not evidence of mathematical correction.

key_findings.claim: As a 2026 field reference, the notes are superseded and should be used only as a historical tutorial map.
key_findings.evidence: The bibliography is effectively a 2022 snapshot and omits exact 2022-2026 work on mirror-flow equivalence, stochastic and trajectory-level diagonal bias, current statistical deep-learning surveys, PAC-Bayes and learned-representation bounds, and finite-time generalization. The malformed reproductions make the primary papers safer theorem sources; the notes remain useful for choosing which primary line to read.

method.core_idea: Organize six lectures around the thesis that successful overparameterized learning is governed not only by hypothesis-class capacity but by an algorithm- and parameterization-dependent geometry that selects particular interpolating solutions.
method.mechanism: The notes move from uniform convergence, stability, stochastic optimization, and mirror descent to KKT matching of gradient-flow trajectories. In diagonal linear models, conserved quantities permit an implicit potential in predictor space whose initialization-scale and depth limits interpolate between kernel-like l2 and sparse l1 behavior; separable logistic loss is related to margin maximization.
assumptions: The expository classical results require the convexity, boundedness, Lipschitzness, compactness, confidence, and projection assumptions of their original sources even where the notes omit them.

The exact square-loss implicit-bias examples use continuous-time gradient flow, linear predictors, diagonal or commuting parameterizations, balanced initialization, interpolation, and convergence to zero training error.
The depth-two hypentropy result assumes beta=w-plus squared minus w-minus squared and balanced positive initialization of scale alpha.
The deep diagonal formula from the primary source requires D at least 3; D=2 is a separate logarithmic/hypentropy case.
The width-dependent matrix result in its valid primary form assumes commuting measurements and a controlled joint width/initialization limit.

The logistic max-margin line requires separable data, exponential-tail loss, homogeneity and smoothness conditions, loss convergence to zero, and directional convergence under an admissible optimization regime.
The lecture figures are primarily explanatory and do not define a reproducible experimental protocol.

techniques.role: Frames inductive bias using ERM, hypothesis complexity, VC/Rademacher ideas, and computational learnability.
Reviews interpolation, effective-rank intuition, and double-descent narratives for noisy overparameterized regression.
Uses leave-one-out and replace-one-out stability to connect regularized empirical optimization with expected generalization.
Relates strongly convex potentials and Lipschitz losses to algorithmic stability and geometry-dependent sample complexity.
Presents mirror descent, Bregman geometry, dual updates, and linearized FTRL as a common optimization language.
Pushes parameter gradient flow through a predictor map and interprets the resulting preconditioner as a function-space metric or tangent kernel.
Matches trajectory invariants and interpolation constraints to KKT conditions of an implicit regularization problem.
Solves balanced diagonal linear-network gradient flow using conserved coordinate products and integrated residuals.
Uses the hypentropy potential to interpolate between l2-like kernel bias and l1-like rich bias as initialization scale varies.
Discusses lifted symmetric matrix factorization and joint width/initialization scaling under commuting measurements.
Extends the diagonal construction to homogeneous depth D and compares implicit with explicit quasi-norm bias.
Connects separable logistic/exponential loss gradient dynamics to KKT conditions for margin maximization.
Uses 20 static figures to illustrate architectures, level sets, regimes, and selected empirical curves.

evaluations.setting: Rank-two matrix-completion illustration comparing direct optimization over X with full-rank factorization X=UV transpose.
evaluations.metric: Relative squared error against a null predictor across the displayed procedures.
evaluations.result: The factorized procedures visually outperform direct X optimization and vary with the optimization variant.
evaluations.baseline: Direct gradient descent on X; the caption and source provide no complete protocol, seeds, uncertainty, or data generator.

evaluations.setting: A hidden-width sweep from roughly 4 to 4096 units.
evaluations.metric: Training and test error at convergence.
evaluations.result: Training error reaches zero around width 64 and test error continues decreasing before flattening near 0.016.
evaluations.baseline: Widths are compared with one curve each; task identity, optimizer, seeds, repeated trials, and numerical table are absent.

evaluations.setting: Conceptual polynomial underfitting/overfitting and double-descent diagrams.
evaluations.metric: Schematic training and test error versus model size or complexity.
evaluations.result: The diagrams illustrate an interpolation peak and a later descending regime.
evaluations.baseline: These are explanatory cartoons rather than measurements and carry no dataset or uncertainty.

evaluations.setting: Depth-two diagonal sparse regression with d=1000, five planted nonzeros, n=100, and Gaussian label noise variance 0.01.
evaluations.metric: Population error and excess l1/l2 norm as initialization scale alpha varies.
evaluations.result: Small alpha is shown with low population error and l1 excess, while large alpha approaches a poor minimum-l2 interpolator.
evaluations.baseline: Rich versus linear-kernel limit; the notes include no code, seeds, repetitions, intervals, y ticks, or exact generator.

evaluations.setting: Sparse-regression sample-count sweep for the largest alpha attaining population error at most 0.025.
evaluations.metric: Threshold initialization scale alpha versus m, with an l1 sample threshold marker.
evaluations.result: The threshold grows with sample count after an apparent vertical asymptote.
evaluations.baseline: Minimum-l1 sample threshold; the plot has no raw values, uncertainty, or reproducible search protocol.

evaluations.setting: Analytic comparison of the implicit hypentropy coordinate potential q and explicit parameter-distance branch r.
evaluations.result: The selected plotted branches are close but differ, supporting different approach rates to l1.
evaluations.baseline: Analytic q versus an unstated branch of a quartic r; the text falsely calls the real root unique.

evaluations.setting: Analytic depth sweep for diagonal homogeneous networks.
evaluations.metric: Shape of the implicit coordinate cost q_D for multiple depths.
evaluations.result: The intended primary-source curves show a faster polynomial transition toward the rich limit for D greater than 2.
evaluations.baseline: Depth two versus deeper analytic potentials; the notes' printed h_D is identically zero, so the source equations cannot regenerate the image.

evaluations.setting: Finite-accuracy depth-two diagonal classification with initialization scale alpha=2.
evaluations.metric: Schematic predictor trajectory relative to minimum-l2, minimum-l1, and Q_alpha margin paths, annotated epsilon=10^-1700.
evaluations.result: The figure suggests traversal near a Q_alpha path before the asymptotic l1 endpoint.
evaluations.baseline: Analytic limit landmarks only; the caption explicitly says the path is unproved and gives no experiment specification.

evaluations.setting: Clean rebuild of the exact current TeX source archive.
evaluations.metric: Compilation completion, page count, figure inclusion, and warnings.
evaluations.result: LaTeX reproduces a 66-page document with all 20 figures and no fatal build error.
evaluations.baseline: The official current PDF has the same page count; compilation validates assembly only, not theorem correctness or curve generation.

limitations: The document is a tutorial transcription of 2022 lectures rather than original research, but its broad title can obscure that status.
Dozens of equations are mistyped, dimensionally invalid, sign-reversed, or copied with identical plus/minus branches, including central stability, mirror, width, depth, and logistic derivations.
The exact implicit-bias calculations concern linear diagonal or commuting models under continuous gradient flow and do not establish analogous behavior for realistic deep networks.
Many classical bounds omit boundedness, Lipschitzness, convexity, compact-domain, confidence, projection, or distribution assumptions.
The notes conflate implicit parameter bias, predictor-space norm, algorithmic selection, and population generalization even though one does not automatically imply the others.
Several results are reproduced less accurately than their cited primary papers, so theorem-level reuse requires returning to those sources.
All empirical-looking plots are static images without code, raw data, seeds, repetitions, confidence intervals, or full protocols.
Several plots omit y-axis tick values or are axisless schematics, preventing quantitative extraction.
The source has no test suite, environment, figure generators, or machine-readable tables.
The bibliography is effectively a 2022 snapshot and omits substantial 2022-2026 work on the exact topics presented.
The matrix-factorization and deep-diagonal claims require commutativity, balanced initialization, interpolation, and convergence assumptions that are easy to miss in the prose.
The logistic discussion treats separability as automatic from d greater than n and overstates KKT limit points as global minimum-norm solutions.
The survey gives limited treatment to PAC-Bayes, compression, data-dependent margins, SGD noise, finite-time dynamics, learned representations, or nonasymptotic deep-network generalization.
The current journal-version status does not imply that the displayed equations were corrected; current arXiv v2 retains the audited defects.
Draft comments in the official source reveal unresolved transcription and proof-writing notes adjacent to several broken passages.
failure_modes: A reader copies Lecture 4's plus-sign Bregman divergence and obtains a quantity that can be negative.
A stability proof is reused without convex losses, so adding a strongly convex regularizer does not make the full nonconvex objective strongly convex.
The growing B square-root t SGD step is implemented, causing divergence while being mistaken for a standard optimal schedule.
A fixed-training-set stochastic gradient is treated as unbiased for population risk rather than empirical risk.
The reciprocal diagonal preconditioner is used, reversing the rich dynamics and contradicting the hypentropy Hessian.
The mistranscribed Woodworth theorem is cited for a wrong l2 comparator or wrong alpha threshold.
The width bullets classify the same limit as both rich and kernel because big-O overlaps little-o and the zero lifted scale is reversed.
The identically zero h_D is inverted or plotted, silently importing a result that the written equations cannot generate.
D=2 is substituted into formulas dividing by D minus 2.
The l_{2/D} quasi-norm is described as less sparse than l1, reversing the intended comparison.
Labels omitted from logistic gradients and KKT stationarity yield a separator supported by unsigned examples.
The positive exponential sign makes high-margin points dominate, the opposite of the support-vector asymptotic argument.
A KKT stationary point in a nonconvex homogeneous network is reported as the unique global minimum-norm classifier.
Static teaching figures are treated as reproduced experiments despite having no generators or uncertainty.
A broad modern-deep-learning claim is inferred from diagonal linear gradient flow without causal or empirical validation in nonlinear networks.
Successful TeX compilation is mistaken for mathematical or experimental reproducibility.
reusable_insights: Separate three questions explicitly: which interpolator an optimizer selects, what predictor-space complexity that selection induces, and whether that complexity guarantees population generalization.
Mirror descent is a valuable common language only when the Bregman sign, mirror-map domain, projection, and primal/dual dimensions are checked locally.
For a parameterization beta=F(w), derive the function-space dynamics directly as J J transpose times the gradient before naming a metric or its inverse.
Balanced diagonal networks are a clean laboratory because conserved coordinate products permit exact predictor-space potentials.
Initialization scale, width, depth, training time, and loss accuracy are distinct control parameters whose limit ordering matters.
Kernel-versus-rich labels should be attached to measurable dynamics or predictors, not inferred solely from parameter count or initialization magnitude.
KKT matching is a useful endpoint technique but needs convergence, feasibility, constraint qualification, convexity or an explicit stationary-point qualification.
When reproducing a theorem in lecture notes, retain the exact comparator, scaling variable, domain, and sufficiency-versus-necessity language from the primary source.
A visual audit should distinguish analytic plots, conceptual schematics, copied demonstrations, and genuinely reproducible experiments.
Static source images are not evidence artifacts; plot generators, raw values, seeds, and uncertainty must accompany empirical claims.
Commutativity is a structural boundary: it enables scalar/spectral integration, while noncommutative matrix flow can have path-order dependence and qualitatively larger reachable sets.
Tutorial syntheses remain useful navigation aids even when current primary surveys and sharper results supersede their theorem coverage.
open_questions: Can the six lectures be formally corrected into a machine-checked companion whose displays agree with every cited primary theorem?
Which optimizer-dependent predictor complexities yield nonvacuous, data-dependent generalization guarantees for realistic nonlinear networks?
What are necessary and sufficient conditions for a reparameterized gradient flow to be exactly equivalent to mirror flow in predictor space?
How do discrete step size, minibatch noise, momentum, and adaptive preconditioning change diagonal-network endpoint and trajectory bias?
Can width and initialization transitions be characterized for noncommuting matrix measurements beyond the kernel extreme?
How do finite-time and finite-accuracy biases differ from asymptotic margin or interpolation limits at practical losses?
Which implicit-bias claims survive feature-learning nonlinearities, multiple layers, nonseparable data, and realistic augmentation?
Can stability, PAC-Bayes, compression, and margin accounts be unified with evolving representation geometry rather than fixed hypothesis classes?
What experimental protocol can distinguish l1-like feature selection from ordinary kernel adaptation while controlling compute and optimization accuracy?
When does benign interpolation coexist with a provably simple individual predictor rather than merely favorable distributional averaging?
Can source-to-source theorem transcription checks automatically flag sign, branch, dimension, and comparator drift in surveys and lecture notes?
What current curriculum best preserves the notes' pedagogical arc while replacing malformed and obsolete sections with verified primary results?

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization
competitive_landscape.difference: Provides the random-label and memorization evidence that motivates modern generalization theory; it is an empirical challenge rather than the target's mirror-geometry tutorial.

competitive_landscape.title: Computing Nonvacuous Generalization Bounds for Deep (Stochastic) Neural Networks with Many More Parameters than Training Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Develops numerically nonvacuous PAC-Bayes and MDL bounds for deep stochastic networks, a major line largely absent from the notes.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Regularization in Matrix Factorization
competitive_landscape.difference: Introduces the nuclear-norm conjecture and evidence for matrix factorization; later counterexamples make its scope more conditional than several lecture summaries imply.

competitive_landscape.title: Spectrally-normalized margin bounds for neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Gives explicit multiclass spectral-norm and margin bounds plus experiments on realistic networks instead of a broad informal capacity narrative.

competitive_landscape.title: Exploring Generalization in Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Compares norm, sharpness, robustness, and PAC-Bayes measures and emphasizes normalization, rather than assuming one optimizer-induced norm explains generalization.

competitive_landscape.title: A PAC-Bayesian Approach to Spectrally-Normalized Margin Bounds for Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Combines PAC-Bayes with spectral normalization and margins, filling a major omission under the target's broad statistical-learning title.

competitive_landscape.title: The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Separable Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Proves linear separable max-margin behavior under explicit conditions; the notes omit labels and signs and overextend the result to arbitrary homogeneous networks.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Linear Convolutional Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Establishes Fourier-domain l_{2/L} bias for linear convolutional networks with precise qualifications; the notes provide only a short summary.

competitive_landscape.title: On Lazy Training in Differentiable Programming
competitive_landscape.difference: States precise output scaling, centering, and linearization bounds; the notes' trajectory display suppresses variables and conditions needed for literal equivalence.

competitive_landscape.title: Reconciling modern machine learning practice and the bias-variance trade-off
competitive_landscape.difference: Provides an empirical and conceptual double-descent synthesis; the target compresses this lineage into a schematic and subjective history claim.

competitive_landscape.title: Generalization in Deep Networks: The Role of Distance from Initialization
competitive_landscape.difference: Develops initialization-dependent capacity bounds more carefully than the notes' blanket statements about staying close and minimizing a norm.

competitive_landscape.title: Surprises in High-Dimensional Ridgeless Least Squares Interpolation
competitive_landscape.difference: Provides quantitative high-dimensional ridgeless risk and double-descent theory, whereas the target gives a short qualitative effective-rank account.

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient Descent Maximizes the Margin of Homogeneous Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Characterizes KKT limit points under detailed assumptions; it does not justify the notes' unconditional global minimum-l2 language.

competitive_landscape.title: Benign Overfitting in Linear Regression
competitive_landscape.difference: Gives effective-rank conditions for benign interpolation; the target summarizes the intuition without reproducing the precise spectral conditions.

competitive_landscape.title: Fantastic Generalization Measures and Where to Find Them
competitive_landscape.difference: Tests more than 40 measures across 10,000 networks and directly asks whether proposed complexities track generalization, a validation layer absent from the notes.

competitive_landscape.title: Kernel and Rich Regimes in Overparametrized Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Supplies the exact hypentropy, depth, and width theorems reproduced in Lectures 5-6; comparison exposes mistranscribed comparators, scales, and identical branches in the notes.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Bias in Deep Linear Classification: Initialization Scale vs Training Accuracy
competitive_landscape.difference: Analyzes the diagonal-classification limit ordering and extremely late asymptotics that the target reduces to an unparameterized schematic.

competitive_landscape.title: Benign overfitting in ridge regression
competitive_landscape.difference: Sharpens bias-variance analysis, removes independence restrictions, and studies negative ridge, advancing beyond the lecture snapshot.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards an Understanding of Benign Overfitting in Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Provides a two-layer ReLU near-minimax benign-overfitting result, moving beyond the target's mostly linear effective-rank discussion.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Bias of SGD for Diagonal Linear Networks: a Provable Benefit of Stochasticity
competitive_landscape.difference: Characterizes an SGD-specific diagonal-network bias and benefit of stochasticity, which the target's gradient-flow treatment largely erases.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Sparse Regularization: The Impact of Depth and Early Stopping
competitive_landscape.difference: Studies noisy and correlated sparse regression plus early stopping, materially broadening the target's noiseless endpoint potential story.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Reparametrized Models: On Equivalence to Mirror Descent
competitive_landscape.difference: Gives exact commuting-parameterization and Legendre-map conditions for mirror equivalence, formalizing the central heuristic that the notes present with sign and typing errors.

competitive_landscape.title: Incremental Learning in Diagonal Linear Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Studies incremental support activation along the trajectory rather than only an endpoint implicit potential.

competitive_landscape.title: Saddle-to-Saddle Dynamics in Diagonal Linear Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Provides a near-complete vanishing-initialization trajectory and LARS-like jumps, a direct advance omitted from the current lecture-note revision.

competitive_landscape.title: A Survey on Statistical Theory of Deep Learning: Approximation, Training Dynamics, and Generative Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Covers approximation, NTK/mean-field training, and generative models with a broader and more current literature map than the target's 2022 lecture scope.

competitive_landscape.title: Get rich quick: exact solutions reveal how unbalanced initializations promote rapid feature learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Uses exact linear and nonlinear solutions to study layer imbalance and feature-learning speed, extending the balanced-scale story.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Bias of Mirror Flow on Separable Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Develops horizon-function max-margin results for broad mirror potentials, a rigorous successor to the target's Euclidean-heavy classification sketch.

competitive_landscape.title: Mathematical theory of deep learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Provides a much broader rigorous book covering approximation, optimization, and statistical learning, superseding the target as a field overview.

competitive_landscape.title: Lecture Notes on Linear Neural Networks: A Tale of Optimization and Generalization in Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Focuses on linear-network dynamical tools and exercises with a newer reference base and more explicit optimization machinery.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Bias of Mirror Flow for Shallow Neural Networks in Univariate Regression
competitive_landscape.difference: Lifts mirror-flow analysis from diagonal linear toys to variational function-space bias in wide shallow nonlinear regression.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards A Unified PAC-Bayesian Framework for Norm-based Generalization Bounds
competitive_landscape.difference: Develops anisotropic, structure-aware PAC-Bayes norm bounds, offering a current alternative to the notes' crude capacity-to-norm story.

competitive_landscape.title: A Theory of Generalization in Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Links evolving tangent kernels, minibatch training, benign overfitting, feature learning, and grokking nonasymptotically, beyond the target's fixed-kernel and endpoint accounts.

competitive_landscape.title: Pointwise Generalization in Deep Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Uses learned representations and Riemannian dimension for pointwise bounds rather than fixed size or norm accounts.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Bias of Mirror Flow in Homogeneous Neural Networks: Sparse and Dense Feature Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Shows how mirror maps shape sparse and dense learned representations with rates, extending the target's stationary classifier discussion.

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient Flow Dynamics and Implicit Bias of Diagonal Linear Networks under Infinitesimal Initialization
competitive_landscape.difference: Characterizes gradient-flow dynamics, modified-l1 endpoints, and invariant structure under infinitesimal initialization for broader diagonal settings.

competitive_landscape.title: Nearly-tight VC-dimension and pseudodimension bounds for piecewise linear neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Proves depth- and unit-dependent bounds such as O(WL log W), correcting the target's suppression of depth and its conflation of sign and ReLU capacity statements.

competitive_landscape.title: Characterizing Implicit Bias in Terms of Optimization Geometry
competitive_landscape.difference: Directly studies mirror, natural-gradient, and steepest-descent bias for underdetermined regression and separable classification; it is the most important omitted precursor to the notes' optimization-geometry framework and records corrected matrix-factorization scope in its revision history.

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient descent aligns the layers of deep linear networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Provides rigorous risk convergence, layer alignment, and end-to-end max-margin direction under stated logistic gradient-flow/GD conditions; it does not support an algorithm- and loss-independent minimum-l2 claim.

competitive_landscape.title: Disentangling feature and lazy training in deep neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Studies the joint width/scale crossover, evolving kernels, and architecture/data-dependent performance, complicating the notes' mostly one-dimensional large-versus-small initialization story.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Regularization in Deep Matrix Factorization
competitive_landscape.difference: Shows depth can strengthen low-rank bias while simple norm or quasi-norm accounts may be insufficient, counterbalancing the notes' fixed-potential framing.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent for Wide Two-layer Neural Networks Trained with the Logistic Loss
competitive_landscape.difference: Analyzes homogeneous activations, exponential-tail loss, and infinite-width measure dynamics under explicit limiting assumptions; the notes' claim of initialization- and learning-rate independence erases this scope.

competitive_landscape.title: Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Classifies parameterizations into kernel and feature-learning limits and constructs infinite-width feature-learning dynamics, showing there is no single canonical infinite-size network.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Resolving the Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent for Matrix Factorization: Greedy Low-Rank Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Constructs counterexamples to the nuclear-norm conjecture and proposes greedy low-rank dynamics, limiting claims that one fixed mirror potential universally captures factorized gradient flow.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Implicit Bias of Initialization Shape: Beyond Infinitesimal Mirror Descent
competitive_landscape.difference: Shows that relative layer and weight scales, not only one scalar magnitude, change the learned regularizer, directly challenging the notes' ranking of optimization choices as least significant.

competitive_landscape.title: Benign Overfitting of Constant-Stepsize SGD for Linear Regression
competitive_landscape.difference: Finds SGD-specific effective dimension and dependence on the initial iterate, constant step, and averaging, showing benignity is not solely a property of minimum-norm ERM covariance.

competitive_landscape.title: The Interplay Between Implicit Bias and Benign Overfitting in Two-Layer Linear Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Couples gradient-flow implicit bias to excess risk and shows initialization quality and covariance jointly matter, whereas the target separates benign overfitting from its later bias analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: The Implicit Bias of Benign Overfitting
competitive_landscape.difference: Shows minimum-norm interpolation can be inconsistent under misspecification while max-margin classification can behave differently, qualifying broad claims that minimum-complexity interpolation is harmless.

competitive_landscape.title: Benign Overfitting in Two-layer Convolutional Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Gives an SNR-controlled sharp benign-versus-harmful phase transition in a nonlinear CNN, showing that nonlinear characterizations already existed before the lectures even though no fully general theory did.

competitive_landscape.title: Self-Consistent Dynamical Field Theory of Kernel Evolution in Wide Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Derives deterministic dynamic order parameters for hidden-feature and tangent-kernel evolution, providing nonlinear theory beyond the notes' diagonal models.

competitive_landscape.title: Mirror Descent Maximizes Generalized Margin and Can Be Implemented Efficiently
competitive_landscape.difference: Rigorously characterizes p-mirror descent's generalized max-margin direction and efficient implementation, strengthening the target's informal classification discussion.

competitive_landscape.title: Benign overfitting in leaky ReLU networks with moderate input dimension
competitive_landscape.difference: Connects approximate margin maximization to benign and harmful phases at moderate dimension; v1 was available before the target's current v2 and strengthens the nonlinear frontier.

competitive_landscape.title: Leveraging Continuous Time to Understand Momentum When Training Diagonal Linear Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Characterizes how step size and momentum combine into an intrinsic trajectory scale and affect sparse recovery, filling the target's omission of momentum and discrete optimizer controls.

competitive_landscape.title: Criteria and Bias of Parameterized Linear Regression under Edge of Stability Regime
competitive_landscape.difference: Studies parameterized regression beyond the classical small-step regime and makes edge-of-stability bias explicit, outside the target's continuous-gradient-flow account.

competitive_landscape.title: From Kernels to Features: A Multi-Scale Adaptive Theory of Feature Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Bridges changes in kernel scale and data-adaptive kernel direction through a multi-scale theory, going beyond a binary fixed-kernel versus rich-potential picture.

competitive_landscape.title: Adaptive kernel predictors from feature-learning infinite limits of neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Shows that feature-learning infinite-width regimes can themselves yield data-dependent kernel predictors, blurring the target's kernel-versus-rich dichotomy.

competitive_landscape.title: Feature learning is decoupled from generalization in high capacity neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Distinguishes feature-learning strength from feature quality and shows stronger feature learning need not explain generalization, directly qualifying the target's feature-learning rhetoric.

competitive_landscape.title: High-dimensional Limit of SGD for Diagonal Linear Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Derives high-dimensional SDE and deterministic state evolution for SGD on diagonal linear networks, replacing the target's noise-free gradient-flow endpoint with explicit drift and gradient-noise dynamics.

competitive_landscape.title: Benign interpolation and Occam's razor
competitive_landscape.difference: Argues that calling an individual interpolator simple does not replace a theorem connecting simplicity to generalization, directly qualifying the notes' rhetoric.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The lectures aim to overview central questions in applying statistical learning theory to deep learning and to build a detailed framework connecting mirror geometry with implicit bias and kernel-versus-feature-learning regimes in diagonal linear models.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The current document is explicitly derived from 2022 Les Houches lectures. Its central exact theorems and examples are credited reproductions of prior work, especially Woodworth et al. for diagonal square-loss models and Soudry, Nacson, and Lyu-Li for margin bias. No new code, theorem, experiment, or dataset is supplied.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is pedagogical organization, not research priority: a readable historical tutorial path from classical SLT to implicit-bias geometry. It should not be cited as the authoritative theorem source because current v2 materially mistranscribes several central results, and it is superseded as a 2026 survey by broader and more rigorous references.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text audit completed 2026-08-24 against every page of the current arXiv:2311.15404v2 manuscript (66 pages, 20 figures), including all displayed definitions, propositions, theorems, proof sketches, numerical illustrations, references, and the July 2022 lecture provenance. All 66 PDF pages were rendered and visually inspected; every source PNG was also inspected at original resolution. Exact source identity was checked against PDF SHA-256 a5cddc383a56c17860ceccb9311577c3bde4994c7340f04ee30ed06fc0fa775f and extracted-text SHA-256 e88acee0d13c1c3cd127129c421c1bcdcce1f5639ca15141ef1ec2f028bc8795. The current arXiv source archive was independently inspected (SHA-256 440d4c9a2f77a5bfecf0c4b6449dce322f5d1496a5c2155ed8849fcc7065e141): it contains TeX, bibliography/styles, auxiliary files, and 20 static PNGs but no code, raw data, environment, tests, or plot generators. A LaTeX build on the audited case-insensitive macOS filesystem succeeded with 66 pages and duplicate-destination/layout warnings; it is not cleanly portable because TeX requests Bregman.png while the archive stores lowercase bregman.png. The current arXiv metadata identifies v2 dated 2024-03-25; the version of record is Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment 2024(10) 104003, DOI 10.1088/1742-5468/ad3a5f, published 2024-10-30. A v1-to-v2 source comparison found mainly editorial expansion, byte-identical PNGs, persistence of the decisive errors, and a newly introduced Bregman-sign error. Central diagonal formulas were compared directly with the official PMLR version of Woodworth et al., arXiv:2002.09277v3, confirming that Theorem 5.1's comparator and threshold, the width scaling, and the deep h_D branches are mistranscribed here. A direct quartic-root check falsified the claimed unique real root; no paper experiment was represented as rerun. The competitive audit verified every listed primary arXiv record at its exact version through the requested 2026-08-23 horizon. This is an absent-only addition; no generated or public projection was rebuilt.
